newsitem.title: UK: Esso sees tight UK petrol margins stabilizing.
newsitem.headline: Esso sees tight UK petrol margins stabilizing.

text.p: Margins in Britain's ferociously competitive petrol market are likely to stabilize at their recently tight levels and keep 1997 site closures near the same rate as in 1996, an Esso Petroleum retailing official said on Monday.

"We would expect sites to continue to close and continue to close at the same rate," Mark Cash, retail planning and economics manager at Esso, a subsidiary of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, told Reuters in an interview.
Cash declined comment on whether Esso was in talks with any supermarkets to join forces in the petrol market, saying only that it "recognized the market potential" for so-called top-up shopping.
Royal Dutch/Shell Group announced in February that it was in talks with one or two British supermarket chains, but did not name them.
Esso, the largest U.K. retailer with about 2,000 filling stations and a total of 10,000 in Europe, launched its Pricewatch campaign in early 1996 promising to match its lowest priced competitors.
The ensuing price war squeezed margins to as low as two pence per litre last summer, sparking estimates that as many as 1,500 to 2,000 sites could close in 1996, for which data are not yet available.
Gross fuel margins were unlikely to fall, at least for a sustained period, to 2 pence per litre, he said, nor return to highs earlier this decade at 6-8 pence.

"With the level of competition today, with the independents, the oil majors and the supermarkets, I don't expect to go back to the historical highs," he said. He added, "I'd be surprised if we went back to the two pence but I expect it to stay pretty tight."

Cash, while warning it was difficult to predict exacly how many sites would go out of business, said U.K. site closures reached as high as 1,400 to 1,500 a year, a rate which could be reached in 1996 and this year.
"Anybody who wants to survive has to live with the margins that the market provides...At the moment, that margin has been dictated by the supermarkets," he said.

Independent oil analysts Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL) said retail margins on unleaded petrol narrowed to 4.7 pence per litre for major brand operators in mid-February, down from five pence in January.
Auto diesel margins recovered slightly in Februrary to five pence per litre from 4.6 pence in December, due to a sharp drop in spot gas oil prices.
World oil prices, including spot prices for Northwest Europe gasoline cargoes, fell sharply in the last two weeks to their lowest levels since the third quarter of 1996.
